title: After a Head Hit, Keep Two Sets of Notes
subtitle: A friend can help notice changes, get care and make recovery easier to track—without trying to diagnose a concussion.
imageAlt: Two adult siblings sit at a kitchen table, one writing down observations after a head injury while the other rests nearby.
imageConcept: A quiet, everyday scene with two adult friends or siblings at a kitchen table: one taking notes on a phone or notepad while the other sits comfortably. No examination, ice pack theatrics or distressed expressions; the mood is attentive and practical.
body:
After an adult hits their head, the first job is not to work out whether they have a concussion. It is to notice whether they need emergency help. Call 911 or go to an emergency department for danger signs such as repeated vomiting, a headache that gets worse, a seizure, slurred speech, unusual behavior or difficulty waking. Do not spend time completing a checklist, searching online or waiting to see whether symptoms pass before getting help. If you are unsure what to do, call 911 and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) lists these and other adult warning signs as reasons to seek emergency care. [1]

A friend can be useful here by staying focused on what is happening, helping make the call and sharing clear observations. The role is support, not diagnosis.
A concussion does not require a blackout

A head injury can be serious even if the person never lost consciousness. Symptoms may be subtle at first, and they can show up right away or hours or days later. A person might seem briefly dazed, have a headache, feel dizzy or nauseated, become unusually tired, or have trouble concentrating or remembering. Those changes deserve attention, but no single sign—or absence of a sign—lets a friend confirm or rule out concussion. [1]

That uncertainty is one reason first aid should not become an improvised neurological exam. The 2024 American Heart Association and American Red Cross first-aid guidelines say there is no validated scoring system for identifying concussion in the first-aid setting. If concussion signs or symptoms appear during an activity, the person should stop and not return until evaluated by a health-care professional. [2] A calm, plain description of what you saw is more useful than a confident label.

Once immediate danger has been addressed, a companion can help preserve details the injured person may later find hard to recall. Write down when the impact happened, what the person was doing, what part of the head was struck if known, and what changed afterward. Record the time you noticed each symptom and whether it seemed to improve, persist or worsen. Include relevant details such as a fall, collision or other impact, using observable language rather than interpretation: “asked the same question twice” is clearer than “seemed confused.”

Keep the record brief and factual. It can be a note on paper or a phone, as long as the person is comfortable with you keeping it. A clinician can use this account alongside their own assessment; it is not a home test and should never delay emergency care. If the person does not want you to record details, respect that and offer to help them remember what they want to share.
Help connect the person with care

If there are no emergency warning signs, help the person contact a health-care professional for guidance about the injury and next steps. Offer practical support: find the number they want to call, help describe what happened, arrange a ride if needed, or sit with them while they speak with a clinician. Let the injured person lead whenever they can. They may want company, help with logistics, or privacy—and those preferences can change.

The CDC’s recovery guidance advises contacting a health-care provider if symptoms last beyond two to three weeks, or worsen after a return to usual activities. That is a follow-up threshold, not a reason to postpone getting advice after a head injury. A clinician can advise what assessment or follow-up is appropriate for this person. [3] If new emergency warning signs appear at any point, switch from note-taking to emergency help.
If they go home after emergency care

Follow the instructions given by the treating team, rather than relying on a generic monitoring rule. 

Before leaving care, help make sure the person knows which symptoms require urgent action, whom to contact with questions, and what activities or medicines the clinician has addressed. If instructions are unclear, ask the care team to explain them before you leave. A companion can write down answers, but the person who was injured should be included in the conversation and in decisions about sharing their information.
Let recovery be gradual, not a test of toughness

After a mild traumatic brain injury or concussion, the CDC describes a short initial period of rest followed by a gradual return to activity. If symptoms get worse as activity increases, scale back and follow the health-care provider’s guidance. Avoid activities that could lead to another head injury while recovering. [3] The right pace is individual; a friend should not push someone to resume work, exercise, driving or social plans simply because they look better or want to prove they are fine.

Make support concrete and adjustable. You might offer to bring food, help with a necessary errand, or check whether the person wants a quieter visit. Ask before taking over tasks or contacting others. Keep the person’s own instructions visible and help them track changes only if they want that assistance. If a new symptom appears, a familiar symptom worsens, or the recovery plan is not working, contact the health-care provider; emergency warning signs still call for emergency care.

Two people can reduce the chance that important details get lost between the impact, a call for advice and a follow-up visit. One person can focus on staying with the injured adult while the other, if welcome, makes a call or records the timeline. If you are alone, prioritize the person and emergency instructions over documentation. Share notes only with the people the injured adult chooses or with clinicians involved in their care.

It also helps to say plainly what you know and what you do not: when the injury happened, what changed, what care has already been sought, and which instructions are still unclear. Avoid promising that everything is fine or predicting how quickly symptoms will resolve. A companion’s steady presence is valuable precisely because it can make room for professional judgment rather than replace it.
Before you put the notes away

At the next calm moment, ask the injured person whether they want a companion to help make a short, dated record for their health-care conversation. Together, note the time and circumstances of the impact, the changes either of you actually observed, when they began, and any care already received. Leave uncertain details marked as uncertain. Then ask what would help with the next step: making a call, getting to an appointment, keeping the notes private, or having some space. If an emergency warning sign appears while you are doing this, stop and call 911—finishing the record can wait. The point is not to produce a complete account; it is to make the next handoff clearer and keep the injured person in charge of their information.
